title: 2 Chronicles 5:1–14
context: With the work finished and David’s dedicated things placed in the treasuries (5:1, parallel 1 Kings 7:51), Solomon gathers Israel’s elders and the whole nation at the feast in the seventh month to bring the ark of the LORD’s covenant up from the City of David (5:2–10, parallel 1 Kings 8:1–9). The ark is set in the most holy place under the cherubim’s wings, and when the priests come out, amid the united praise of singers and trumpeters, the cloud fills the house so that the priests cannot stand to minister (5:11–14, parallel 1 Kings 8:10–11), recalling the tabernacle in Exodus 40:34–35. Differences are named rather than harmonized: 2 Chronicles 5:4 says the Levites took up the ark, where 1 Kings 8:3 says the priests did, in keeping with the Chronicler’s concern in 1 Chronicles 15:2, 15; and 2 Chronicles 5:11b–13a adds the priests’ sanctification without regard to their divisions, the Levite singers, and the song of praise, none of which appears in 1 Kings 8:10. The refrain sung here also appears at 1 Chronicles 16:34, 41 and 2 Chronicles 7:3. Arminian and Reformed readers alike read the glory filling the house as God’s free and gracious act of taking up residence among his people, and they treat the scene as fully shared ground.

verses.text: Thus all the work that Solomon did for the LORD’s house was finished. Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, even the silver, the gold, and all the vessels, and put them in the treasuries of God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: All the work is finished, and Solomon places the silver, gold, and vessels David had dedicated in the treasuries of God’s house, as in 1 Kings 7:51. Arminian readers see father and son joined in one offering: David’s preparation and Solomon’s building together are presented as the gift of a grateful people to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completed work as God’s faithfulness to his word to David that his son would build the house (1 Chronicles 17:11–12). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the hinge between building and dedication, and both stress that what is given to God was first received from his hand.

verses.text: Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the princes of the fathers’ households of the children of Israel, to Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the LORD’s covenant out of David’s city, which is Zion.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon assembles the elders, the heads of the tribes, and the princes of the fathers’ households to bring up the ark from David’s city, which is Zion. Arminian readers see the whole people drawn into the act of worship, with the leaders of every tribe sharing in the joy of bringing God’s ark to its place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the gathering of all Israel’s leadership and see the scene as the fulfillment of David’s desire to build a house of rest for the ark (1 Chronicles 28:2). Shared ground: both traditions read the assembly as a covenant gathering of the whole nation before the LORD, and both find nothing to divide them here.

verses.text: So all the men of Israel assembled themselves to the king at the feast, which was in the seventh month.
verses.arminianNotes: All the men of Israel gather to the king at the feast in the seventh month; Chronicles does not name the month Ethanim as 1 Kings 8:2 does. Arminian readers see the dedication joined to Israel’s festival calendar, so that the people’s regular worship becomes the setting for a new act of God’s grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the timing as tying the dedication to the appointed feasts God gave Israel, which many readers take to be the Feast of Booths held in the seventh month (Leviticus 23:34), though the verse itself does not name the feast. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing the event within ordered covenant worship rather than private devotion.

verses.text: All the elders of Israel came. The Levites took up the ark.
verses.arminianNotes: All the elders come, and the Levites take up the ark, where 1 Kings 8:3 says the priests picked it up. Arminian readers note the difference without resolving it and connect the Chronicler’s wording to David’s ruling that only the Levites should carry God’s ark (1 Chronicles 15:2), learned after the failure at Perez Uzza.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise state the difference plainly and see the Chronicler’s emphasis on worship conducted according to God’s instructions, compare 1 Chronicles 15:15. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that the ark is now handled as God commanded, with reverence rather than presumption.

verses.text: They brought up the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the Tent. The Levitical priests brought these up.
verses.arminianNotes: The ark, the Tent of Meeting, and the holy vessels are brought up, and the verse says the Levitical priests brought these up, where 1 Kings 8:4 says the priests and the Levites. Arminian readers note the difference by reference and see the old tabernacle worship gathered into the new house rather than discarded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same continuity: the God who met Israel at the Tent of Meeting now takes up residence in the house Solomon built. Shared ground: both traditions read the transfer of the tent and vessels as marking one continuous history of worship from Moses to Solomon, ordered by God throughout.

verses.text: King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel who were assembled to him were before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle that could not be counted or numbered for multitude.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon and the assembled congregation sacrifice sheep and cattle beyond counting before the ark. Arminian readers see the extravagant offerings as wholehearted worship, a people pouring out gratitude to God as the ark is brought to its resting place, in a scene of joyful and willing devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the countless sacrifices as worship offered in response to God’s faithfulness, and they note that the sacrifices are offered according to the system God himself provided. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as celebration, and both avoid making the number of offerings a measure of merit.

verses.text: The priests brought in the ark of the LORD’s covenant to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the house, to the most holy place, even under the wings of the cherubim.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests bring the ark into the inner sanctuary, the most holy place, under the wings of the cherubim. Arminian readers note that only the priests enter the most holy place, even though the Levites carried the ark on the way, and they see ordered roles in worship that honor God’s holiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the ark set in its appointed place as the climax of the procession, with God’s throne among his people now fixed in the house built for his name. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the fulfillment of the long journey of the ark, which ends in its resting place.

verses.text: For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covered the ark and its poles above.
verses.arminianNotes: The cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and cover the ark and its poles. Arminian readers see the cherubim as guardians of holiness, a picture of God’s majesty drawn from the tabernacle, and they read the scene as reverent rather than as a puzzle to be decoded in symbolic detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise associate the cherubim with the holiness of God’s throne, as in the tabernacle where God spoke from above the mercy seat between the cherubim (Exodus 25:22). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as description of the most holy place and decline to press its imagery beyond the text.

verses.text: The poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the ark in front of the inner sanctuary, but they were not seen outside; and it is there to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: The poles are long enough that their ends can be seen from the ark in front of the inner sanctuary, though not outside, where 1 Kings 8:8 says from the holy place. Arminian readers note the difference by reference and read the line as an eyewitness-style detail rooted in the house as it once stood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase “it is there to this day” reflects the source the Chronicler is following, a remark many readers take to come from a time before the temple’s destruction, though that is an inference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical detail and decline to build doctrine on it.

verses.text: There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets which Moses put there at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with the children of Israel, when they came out of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Nothing is in the ark except the two tablets Moses placed there at Horeb, when the LORD made a covenant with Israel after the exodus. Arminian readers see the covenant law at the heart of Israel’s worship, a reminder that God’s presence among his people calls for faithful obedience to his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the tablets as the covenant God graciously gave to the people he had redeemed from Egypt, so that the law rests within the context of grace already shown. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing God’s covenant word at the center of the house, under the cherubim.

verses.text: When the priests had come out of the holy place (for all the priests who were present had sanctified themselves, and didn’t keep their divisions;
verses.arminianNotes: As the priests come out of the holy place, the Chronicler adds that all the priests present had sanctified themselves without keeping to their divisions. Arminian readers see a moment so great that every priest prepares to take part, and they note that this addition does not appear in 1 Kings 8:10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the whole priesthood consecrated for the occasion, with the ordinary rotation of service set aside for a unique day of dedication. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of the Chronicler’s fuller account of worship at this moment, which leads to the cloud in 5:13–14.

verses.text: also the Levites who were the singers, all of them, even Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and their brothers, arrayed in fine linen, with cymbals and stringed instruments and harps, stood at the east end of the altar, and with them one hundred twenty priests sounding with trumpets);
verses.arminianNotes: The Levite singers, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun with their families, stand east of the altar in fine linen with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps, joined by one hundred twenty priests with trumpets. Arminian readers see the people’s praise joined in one great act of worship offered freely to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the singers serving in the order David had arranged (1 Chronicles 16:41–42; 25:1), so that worship follows appointed patterns. Shared ground: both traditions note that this detail is an addition not found in 1 Kings 8, and both read it as a picture of ordered, wholehearted praise before the LORD.

verses.text: when the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD; and when they lifted up their voice with the trumpets and cymbals and instruments of music, and praised the LORD, saying, “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever!” then the house was filled with a cloud, even the LORD’s house,
verses.arminianNotes: The trumpeters and singers sound as one, praising the LORD with the words “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever!” and then the cloud fills the house. Arminian readers see God answering his people’s united praise with the gracious gift of his presence, filling the house in response to their worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cloud as God’s sovereign choice to dwell among his people, so that praise is the occasion of his coming rather than its cause. Shared ground: both traditions read the refrain, also found at 1 Chronicles 16:34 and 2 Chronicles 7:3, as confessing God’s steadfast covenant love, the heart of the scene.

verses.text: so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for the LORD’s glory filled God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests cannot stand to minister because of the cloud, for the LORD’s glory fills God’s house. Arminian readers see human service giving way before God’s glory, which overwhelms even those appointed to minister, and they read the moment as one of awe rather than of human accomplishment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene echoing Exodus 40:34–35, where Moses could not enter the Tent of Meeting because of the cloud. Shared ground: both traditions treat the glory filling the house as fully agreed, as at 1 Kings 8:11, and neither draws a contrast from it; it marks God taking up residence among his people.
